name: CIVIC Platform
tagline: A city-scale research platform for evaluating how transportation policies — congestion pricing, transit upgrades, road expansions — reshape air quality and mobility in cities worldwide.
body: Collecting and integrating air quality, transit ridership, and traffic data from cities including NYC, London, Stockholm, and São Paulo, then applying causal inference methods to ask whether policy changes actually move the needle on pollution and travel behavior. Students work on data pipelines, panel econometrics, and communicating results to a policy audience.
question: When a city charges drivers to enter its core, does the air actually get cleaner — and who benefits?

name: MOVESAI
tagline: A machine-learning short-form surrogate of the EPA's MOVES vehicle emissions simulator — fast, queryable, and deployable.
body: MOVES is powerful but heavy. MOVESAI learns a compact surrogate model that reproduces its emissions outputs at a fraction of the runtime, wrapped in an API and front-end so others can actually use it — then writes the whole thing up.
question: Can a LightGBM model learn MOVES well enough to run 100× faster without losing accuracy?

name: BIKESHARE
tagline: A real-time data pooling system for every public bikeshare feed in the world — so cities can finally be compared on equal footing.
body: Hundreds of cities publish live bikeshare feeds, but no one has pooled them into a single queryable system. This project builds that infrastructure: continuously ingesting GBFS feeds, unifying schema across operators, and exposing a clean API for evaluating and comparing bikeshare performance — ridership patterns, utilization, coverage gaps, equity — across cities worldwide.
question: Can we build a real-time data pooling system for all the public bikeshare data in the world?

name: Climate Action in Transportation (CAT)
tagline: A dashboard system that lets local decision-makers estimate transportation emissions online — without running MOVES locally.
body: Lead software developer & coordinator on a multi-million-dollar US-DOT-funded effort at Cornell with Dr. Oliver Gao. We build the dashboards, databases, APIs, and cloud jobs that turn EPA MOVES into a public-facing emissions tool. MEng students contribute to CAT VISUALIZER, the policy optimizer, and the underlying API.

name: Social Infrastructure & Emergency Mobility
tagline: Measuring how community spaces — parks, libraries, places of worship — shape a city's ability to prepare for and recover from disasters.
body: Cities with denser social infrastructure bounce back faster from hurricanes, floods, and pandemics — but how much, and where? Students build spatial analysis pipelines to score social infrastructure across 25 major US cities, then link those scores to evacuation behavior (drawn from cell-phone mobility data) and hazard exposure. The work spans a Shiny dashboard, a Plumber API, and Supabase-backed data storage.
question: Does where your neighbors gather predict how well your city survives a disaster?

name: FaultDB
tagline: A web platform for building and analyzing fault trees and attack trees — reliability engineering made usable, open to MEng contributors.
body: Reliability engineers spend too long fighting desktop software. FaultDB pairs an R compute engine (the tidyfault package) with a React + React Flow diagram editor and a Supabase backend so teams can build fault trees, run cut-set analysis, and extract top-event probabilities from a browser. MEng students work on the analysis algorithms, the interactive diagram UI, and the API connecting them.
question: What is the probability that this system fails — and which components matter most?

name: Social Infrastructure Mapping
tagline: Mapping community spaces that build social capital — across Boston, Fukuoka, and the 25 largest US cities.
body: With colleagues at Northeastern and MIT, mapping community-level places (parks, libraries, places of worship, social businesses) using the Google Maps Places API + ground-truthing, then linking to pandemic, mobility, and resilience outcomes. Now in expansion phase with Cornell undergraduates across US cities.

name: Evacuation with Mobility Data
tagline: Estimating evacuation from hurricanes, wildfires, earthquakes, and floods using anonymized cell-phone movement data.
body: Replacing roadside / post-hoc surveys with passive mobility data to measure who evacuates, where they go, and what predicts that flow — Hurricane Dorian, the 2018 Hokkaido earthquake, Hurricane Zeta, the Glass Fire, COVID-era evacuation, and more.

name: Polarization & Health
tagline: Two national surveys testing how partisan polarization shapes Americans' physical and mental well-being.
body: Drafted and administered two nationwide surveys on trust, polarization, and health. Findings: cross-party division is linked to worse health outcomes; close in-group ties buffer that effect; polarization also predicts COVID-19 vaccination uptake.
